title: How Much Do You Hide Your True Self?
author: Arthur C. Brooks
summary: In this weekly happiness newsletter, Arthur Brooks reflects on the masks people wear at Halloween and in ordinary life. He grants that masking can be healthy and freeing, citing the German word Maskenfreiheit for the freedom found behind a mask. The problem arises when masking becomes permanent and central to work or life, which researchers call emotional labor and link to lower well-being. He offers three rules for taking the mask off: take a regular break from yourself, remove the mask around the people you love most, and make sure you like what is behind it. On the last point he notes that self-acceptance lowers anxiety and that disliked personality traits can be changed with honesty and deliberate effort. The newsletter body is short, and the longer Free Press column and the podcast episode it points to were not archived. It is filed under Leadership because it concerns authenticity and emotional labor at work and in professional relationships.
points: Masking is healthy in the right contexts, but when it is a permanent part of work or life it becomes costly emotional labor linked to lower well-being.
Take a regular break from yourself, because maintaining an identity takes more energy than most people realise.
Your most important relationships, personal or professional, require you to be yourself, so being masked 24 hours a day is a signal that something needs to change.
If the mask hides things you dislike, such as anger or sadness, keeping it on forfeits the chance to face them, and self-acceptance and honest effort can change traits you do not like.
quotes: In the appropriate contexts, masking your true self can be healthy and freeing. The German language has a special word for the happiness such customs bring: Maskenfreiheit—the freedom found behind a mask.

But when masking is a permanent and central part of your work or life, something is seriously amiss. Researchers call this “emotional labor”—effort exerted just to maintain an acceptable demeanor, which often means suppressing our negative emotions.
Just as a surgical mask can’t be worn 24/7, our metaphorical masks must come off eventually. Here are three rules for doing so.
The energy required to maintain your identity is probably greater than you realize, and finding a way to relinquish it regularly can help you recharge.

Your most important relationships—the ones in which you invest the lion’s share of your time and energy, whether they’re personal or professional—require you to be able to be yourself. If you are masked up 24 hours a day, something needs to change.
As exhausting as keeping up the mask can be, letting it drop might be a terrifying prospect if you don’t especially like what it’s hiding.
In cases like these, staying masked means missing out on an opportunity to face reality and make some positive changes.
